title: Come to me for refuge
hookLine: after seventeen chapters on duty, Krishna says: come to me for refuge, and do not grieve
carry: take refuge in god, and do not grieve
last: YATHECCHASI — GOD TRUSTS YOU TO CHOOSE.

lines: COME TO ME. I'VE GOT YOU.
cards: A child learning to swim. For weeks: kick like this, cup your hands like that, turn your head, breathe. Rules and more rules.
Then one day the parent stands in the water, arms open, and says: forget all that. Just come to me. I've got you.
The rules weren't wrong. But there's a moment when trust does what technique can't. In one Hindu tradition, the verse right after Krishna hands the choice back is that moment.
They call it the charama shloka, the final verse.

teach.h: ABANDON ALL DHARMAS, COME TO ME.
teach.b: Verse sixty-six. Abandoning all dharmas, come to me alone for refuge. I will free you from all wrongs.
Do not grieve. Sarva-dharman parityajya, mam ekam sharanam vraja. Commentators have argued over every word.
What does abandon all dharmas mean, after a whole book about doing your dharma?

The Sri Vaishnava tradition, which follows Ramanuja, calls this the charama shloka and reads it as surrender, prapatti: stop relying on your own efforts to save yourself, and rely on God's grace alone.

Shankara reads it as renouncing all actions and taking refuge in the one self. Other teachers read dharmas here as your anxieties about merit and demerit, not your duties: keep acting, but let go of the scorekeeping.
However the first line is read, the verse ends with two words: ma shuchah.
Do not grieve. The Gita began with Arjuna grieving, and it ends with Krishna telling him not to. Verses sixty-seven to seventy-one are about passing the teaching on.
Don't tell it to someone who doesn't want to hear it. Whoever shares it with those who love it is most dear. Even someone who only listens with faith, without scoffing, finds freedom.
After all that, Krishna asks: have you heard this with a focused mind, Arjuna?
Is your confusion gone? The teacher checks in. For devotional Hindus this is the heart of bhakti: in the end you aren't saved by getting every rule right.
You lean on God. That's the last instruction: take refuge, don't grieve, and did you hear me?

how: In the Sri Vaishnava tradition, Gita 18.66 is honored as the charama shloka, the final verse, and is central to the teaching of surrender (prapatti); teachers in other traditions also give it a central place.

o: a vow to give up all your duties
refuge, a shelter you can run to
a prayer of thanks after a meal

games.q: the last verse and its readers — tap the pairs.

s: all Hindu teachers read 'abandon all dharmas' the same way
the Sri Vaishnava tradition reads surrender; Shankara reads renouncing action for the self; others read letting go of scorekeeping.
the Gita begins with Arjuna grieving and ends with 'do not grieve'
verse 71 says even someone who just listens with faith finds freedom

games.q: you're Krishna. you've just given the verse Sri Vaishnavas call the final verse. what do you do next?
o: walk away: the teaching is done.
ask Arjuna whether he heard it and whether his confusion is gone.
games.why: verse 72: have you heard this with a focused mind? is your confusion gone? the teacher checks in.

practice: In a hard moment, many Hindus simply say a name of God and lean on it. Notice what you're carrying today: the rules, the scores, the trying to get it all right.
If you pray, say quietly, sharanam, refuge, or a name of God that's yours. If you don't, just set the weight down for a few breaths. Then hear the last two words: do not grieve.

wordCard.voice: Sharanam, refuge, shelter. Gita eighteen, sixty-six: abandoning all dharmas, come to me alone for refuge; I will free you from all wrongs; do not grieve.

orig.note: Sanskrit: sharanam, refuge, shelter; 'mam ekam sharanam vraja', come to me alone for refuge, Gita 18.66.

carryVoice: Your line: take refuge in God, and do not grieve. A book that began in grief ends with ma shuchah. See you tomorrow.
